chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Term Structure of Volatility

lessons.title: Event Risk: How Budget Day, Results Season, and RBI Policy Move the Curve

children.text: Three Recurring Events That Reliably Move the Indian Curve

The last lesson named the event-driven cause of backwardation in general terms. India's calendar has three recurring events that reliably produce it, each with a different scope and a different typical size.

body.caption: Three recurring Indian event-risk sources, compared

cells: Whole market: Nifty, Bank Nifty, and nearly every sector
Large, sharp spike in near-dated index ATM IV in the days before; often the single biggest scheduled index-level event each year
Quarterly, staggered over several weeks each quarter
Individual stocks, and sector indices to a lesser extent
Large spikes in single-stock near-dated ATM IV around each company's own results date; the index-level effect is diluted since companies report on different days
Whole market, with an outsized effect on rate-sensitive sectors like banks, NBFCs, and real estate
A smaller, more moderate curve bump than Budget or major results, since the stance is usually partly pre-signaled through minutes and commentary

children.text: Isolating the Event: How Much of the Curve Is Really "Budget Day"?

A blended 7-day ATM IV that spans the Budget mixes six ordinary trading days with one extraordinary one. Vol traders have a standard way to pull the event day's own contribution out of that blend, using a simple fact: under standard assumptions, variance adds up across days. A week's total variance is just the sum of each individual day's variance. If you know what a normal day contributes and you know the blended total, you can solve for what the one unusual day alone must be contributing.

body.caption: T is the number of trading days in the option's life. IV(blended) is the actual quoted ATM IV for the expiry spanning the event. IV(normal) is what that same expiry's ATM IV would look like on an ordinary week, with no event, the Lesson 1 baseline. The constant that converts variance to its usual annualized form cancels out on both sides, so no separate 252 division is needed here.

children.text: Apply it to Lesson 2's own numbers. Nifty's 7-day ATM IV ahead of the Budget was 18.00%; its normal, non-event 7-day baseline from Lesson 1 was 10.85%.

body.caption: Stripping the Budget day's own implied volatility out of the blended 7-day IV

children.text: Budget day alone is being priced as if it carries roughly 39.5% annualized-equivalent volatility, nearly four times the 10.85% normal daily rate, and well above even the 18% blended weekly figure, exactly as you would expect once you remember that blended number is diluted by six far calmer days. Convert that into a one-day expected move using the Chapter 1 formula, and Nifty at 24,800 with a 39.5% implied event-day vol works out to roughly a ₹513 expected move on Budget day alone, more than the entire week's ordinary expected range from Lesson 1.

body.text: The single most common shortcut mistake here is subtracting IVs directly: 18% minus 10.85% is not the event's contribution to anything meaningful. Volatility does not subtract cleanly; variance does. Skipping the squaring step is the fastest way to badly underestimate how large an event's true implied move actually is.

stats.label: Implied Budget-day volatility
stats.context: Stripped out using the formula above

children.text: Results Season: The Same Technique, One Stock at a Time

Results season is really thousands of small, staggered versions of the exact same phenomenon, one company at a time instead of one whole market at once. Each stock's near-dated weekly options inflate ahead of its own results date, and the identical variance-stripping technique is exactly how single-stock options desks, and increasingly retail platforms like Sensibull, compute the widely quoted "implied earnings move" for a large-cap stock ahead of its results. It is the same formula, applied to one name instead of the index.
RBI Policy: A Smaller, More Frequent Nudge

RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets roughly six times a year, and a rate decision matters most for rate-sensitive sectors like banks, NBFCs, and real estate, with a smaller pull on the broad index. It usually shows up as a real but comparatively modest bump in the near-dated curve, meaningfully smaller than a Budget-day spike, largely because the central bank continuously pre-signals its stance through minutes, speeches, and commentary between meetings, which leaves less genuine surprise left to price in by the time the decision actually lands.

body.title: Applying the formula correctly
body.question: A stock's 5-trading-day option, spanning its earnings announcement, shows a blended ATM IV of 50%, while its normal, non-event ATM IV baseline is 30%. What is the correct next step to estimate the implied volatility of the earnings day itself?
options: Simply subtract: 50% minus 30% equals 20%, the earnings-day implied volatility
Apply sigma-event-squared equals IV-blended-squared times T minus IV-normal-squared times (T minus 1), using T = 5, then take the square root of the result
Average the two figures: (50% plus 30%) divided by 2 equals 40%, the earnings-day implied volatility
The normal baseline IV is irrelevant once you already have the blended IV
body.explanation: Variance, not volatility, adds across days. Subtracting or averaging the IV percentages directly skips the squaring step entirely and badly understates how concentrated the event's true implied move actually is. The variance-stripping formula from this lesson is the only correct way to isolate it.

body.title: Estimating an IT stock's implied earnings move
body.scenario: Ahead of a large IT company's quarterly results, its 4-trading-day weekly option chain shows a blended ATM IV of 45%, against a normal, non-event baseline of 28%. The stock trades at ₹1,640.
body.prompt: Using the variance-stripping method, estimate the implied volatility assigned to results day itself, and the implied one-day expected move on results day. Approximate figures are fine.
body.modelAnswer: Sigma-event-squared equals (0.45 squared times 4) minus (0.28 squared times 3), which is 0.81 minus 0.2352, equal to 0.5748. The square root of 0.5748 is about 75.8%, the annualized-equivalent volatility the market is assigning to results day alone, dramatically higher than either the 28% normal baseline or the 45% blended weekly figure, since that blended figure is diluted by three calmer days. Converting to a one-day expected move: ₹1,640 times 0.758 times the square root of (1 divided by 365) works out to roughly ₹65. So the options market is pricing a one-day move of around ₹65, close to 4% of the stock's price, specifically for results day itself.

body.text: A blended IV that spans an event is never really one number. It is a normal week's worth of ordinary volatility with one extraordinary day mixed in, and variance, not volatility, is what lets you legitimately pull that one day back out and see exactly how large the market thinks it really is.

points: India's three recurring, scheduled sources of event risk are the annual Union Budget (whole market), quarterly results season (stock by stock, staggered), and RBI's roughly six-times-a-year MPC policy (moderate, partly pre-signaled).

Because variance adds across trading days, an event's own implied volatility can be stripped out of a blended IV using sigma-event-squared equals IV-blended-squared times T minus IV-normal-squared times (T minus 1).
Subtracting or averaging IV percentages directly, instead of working through variance, is the most common mistake and badly understates the event's true implied size.

The same variance-stripping technique used for Budget day works identically for a single stock's earnings day, and is how the "implied earnings move" figure shown on platforms like Sensibull is actually computed.
RBI policy decisions move the curve too, but typically by less than a Budget or major results, since ongoing central bank communication pre-signals much of the eventual decision.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All figures, including the Budget-day and results-day calculations, are hypothetical and illustrative, continuing the running Nifty example from earlier chapters, and do not represent live NSE data. The Union Budget's 1 February date and RBI's roughly six-meetings-a-year schedule are general conventions and should be confirmed against the current official calendar. Always check live prices and IV on NSE or your broker's terminal before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
